"It is lack of confidence, more than anything else, that kills a civilisation. We can destroy ourselves by cynicism and disillusion, just as effectively as by bombs." - Kenneth Clark

I think he's confusing a symptom for the illness.

Lack of confidence doesn't just grow in a vacuum. It's a reaction, and generally a wholly justified one, to destructive acts committed by those who would, had they not committed those acts, be rewarded with confidence.

For instance, Americans didn't just wake up one day and decide to not trust their political leaders. Their political leaders, individually and collectively, each and all over the course of their own careers and of their own volition, acted and continue to act in ways that fully justify distrust. In fact, it might be argued that the greatest failing of the American people is that they didn't start distrusting their political leaders long ago, when they were already acting in ways that deserved it.

It might be argued that cynicism and disillusion speed the inevitable collapse, but they don't cause it. The inevitable collapse, just like the cynicism and disillusion, are caused by the overtly destructive acts of people who have been unwisely granted authority.

I disagree. He's talking about the collapse of civilization, not simply distrust in leadership. The kind of cynicism and disillusionment that will convince people there's no point in constructing public works or grand buildings, the cynicism that convinces people to not plant next season's crops.

You have a point in that distrustful leaders undermine confidence in the apparatus that elects leaders and the purpose in electing leaders, but civilization goes on. Confidence in civilization itself is separate from trust in a country's leadership because, after all, the leadership is always changing.

Confidence that your neighbour is a decent person, that people can work together, and that forward progress is possible are all more fundamental than political cynicism or upheaval. France's civilization survived revolutions, and America's civilization survived economic collapse, but when Rome fell, Europe's civilization all but disappeared for hundreds of years. Not only did construction stop, but it went backwards - great monuments were torn down for their materials. The state of architecture took a giant step backward once civilization recovered enough to construct stone buildings again. Knowledge of the structural purpose of roman architectural features was lost, replaced with aesthetic mimicry devoid of understanding.

Edit: Here is an example of the loss of architectural understanding I mentioned: The Baptistère Saint-Jean in Poitiers, France. It's comparatively a rather crude building built around the year 360 and is a neat example of the step back that the Roman collapse caused.

You have a point in that distrustful leaders undermine confidence in the apparatus that elects leaders and the purpose in electing leaders, but civilization goes on.

For a while. Exactly as Rome demonstrated though, it eventually reaches the point at which the leadership is so corrupt and so self-serving and so overtly destructive that the civilization simply cannot continue to withstand their abuses.

And note - I don't mean to even imply that the eventual collapse of civilization is due to political malfeasance exclusively - I'm simply pointing out that political malfeasance is the primary cause of the loss of confidence in the strength of the civilization, so pinning the blame for the inevitable collapse of the civilization on the loss of confidence is akin to ignoring lung cancer and treating the cough.

Confidence in civilization itself is separate from trust in a country's leadership because, after all, the leadership is always changing.

I disagree. Yes - there is at least some degree of separation between the two because, just as you say, the leadership is always changing. But there's much more connection between the two than separation, since the leadership explicitly possesses the authority to determine the arc of the civilization, and to some considerable degree, they do exactly that. And what they do generally has extremely concrete consequences. And, most to the point, the destructive things they do inevitably accumulate and accelerate, since they not only create lasting consequences, that then need to be (though not necessarily are) dealt with - they also each provide precedent for the next, and greater, abuse. Those two things - the accumulation of consequences from past destructive acts and the precedents they establish allowing present and future destructive acts, serve to undermine the civilization as a whole, and thus, and rightly, the citizen's confidence in the civilization as a whole.

Confidence that your neighbour is a decent person, that people can work together, and that forward progress is possible are all more fundamental than political cynicism or upheaval.

Yes, they are, but that doesn't make them separate, or at least not to the degree you're claiming.

As but one example - those living under a police state cannot have total confidence that their neighbor is a decent person, for the very simple reason that there's a very good chance that he in fact is not, and explicitly because that's the environment the government has created.

France's civilization survived revolutions,

So did Rome's.

You make good points, Rottcodd. I still disagree that poor leaders are the primary cause of loss of trust in a civilization. To me a leader is little more than a figurehead since the people are still the generators of goods, services, entertainment, and food.

the leadership explicitly possesses the authority to determine the arc of the civilization

I believe the general will of the people ultimately determines the civilization's arc, the leaders only represent popular will in as much as the people have a choice of leaders. Despots are overthrown if they push too hard, as are unpopular laws. Even police states foster rebellious movements, try as they might to quash them. Examples like American prohibition and China's holey firewall show that people have power over and independence from their leaders even when the leaders are oligarchs or plutarchs or worse.

those living under a police state cannot have total confidence that their neighbor is a decent person, for the very simple reason that there's a very good chance that he in fact is not, and explicitly because that's the environment the government has created

Yes, a police state is a situation where a citizen cannot trust his neighbour, but the loss of trust occurred much earlier, before the police state was instituted, when the citizens internalized fear of their neighbour, not of the state. Then the police state was able to be justified as protection from their fears. The people slowly allowed their freedom to be curtailed in order to alleviate their fears, they willingly invited the police state into power.

I think it's a bit unfair to pin the root cause of collapse mostly on untrustworthy leaders, since it's the people themselves who internalized division and fear. The power of civilization, in my mind, is community, it's grassroots. Leaders don't make or even facilitate civilization, people do, and they do it by choosing cooperation over distrust. Losing community spirit and inclusivity allows a people to be divided and allows fear to spread.

Perhaps it's individualistic culture, emphasizing leaders more than the workers, that breaks people's trust when leader after leader turns out corrupt. A shift in perspective would allow people to see that they can influence the community just as much as a chosen leader and, in fact, leaders only have the power that the community gives them.

Well... I've been down this path before, and experience has shown that at best, it's likely that it's not going to really go anywhere. And I also know from experience that if I continue to pursue it, and you continue to blame the people for what's done to them by those who seek, gain and hold power, there's a pretty good chance that it's going to make me angry, and that wouldn't be worth it.

And the machine will grind on anyway, regardless.

A bit of an addendum in parting though, since something you said reminded me of a quote I particularly like. Regarding the idea that "leaders only have the power that the community gives them":

Find out just what the people will submit to and you have found out the exact amount of injustice and wrong which will be imposed upon them; and these will continue until they are resisted with either words or blows, or with both. The limits of tyrants are prescribed by the endurance of those whom they oppress.

-- Frederick Douglass
